questions.q: When centuries of soot were cleaned from Michelangelo’s frescoes, their original colours proved far brighter than anyone had thought. What does the article compare with this?
options: The fading of human memory
Not quite. The article says: True religion, whose original form has been dimmed by later additions and needs restoring.
The ageing of old buildings
Not quite. The article says: True religion, whose original form has been dimmed by later additions and needs restoring.
True religion, whose original form has been dimmed by later additions and needs restoring
Yes. Then it is seen to be quite different from what was supposed.
The decline of the arts
Not quite. The article says: True religion, whose original form has been dimmed by later additions and needs restoring.
questions.rationale: “In very much the same way, the nature of true religion has become distorted over the centuries… it is in need of restoration to its original form.”

questions.q: How does the article contrast religion in its pure form with religion in a distorted form?
options: Pure religion is simple; distorted religion is complicated
Not quite. The article says: Pure religion springs from the heart and breeds humility and unity; distorted, it becomes empty rites and a source of pride.
Pure religion is private; distorted religion is public
Not quite. The article says: Pure religion springs from the heart and breeds humility and unity; distorted, it becomes empty rites and a source of pride.
Pure religion is old; distorted religion is new
Not quite. The article says: Pure religion springs from the heart and breeds humility and unity; distorted, it becomes empty rites and a source of pride.
Pure religion springs from the heart and breeds humility and unity; distorted, it becomes empty rites and a source of pride
Well read. The spirit is lost while the form remains.
questions.rationale: “Religion in its pristine form breeds humility in its followers, fostering human unity; but when religion becomes distorted, it becomes a source of pride.”

questions.article: Signs of God Scattered in the Universe
questions.q: Most of the earth’s water is salty and undrinkable. Which natural process does the article point to as a sign of God?
options: Evaporation by the sun, which leaves the salt behind and returns the water as fresh rain
Right. Nature’s own desalination.
Ice forming at the poles
Not quite. The article says: Evaporation by the sun, which leaves the salt behind and returns the water as fresh rain.
Springs rising from deep rock
Not quite. The article says: Evaporation by the sun, which leaves the salt behind and returns the water as fresh rain.
Rivers washing salt back to the sea
Not quite. The article says: Evaporation by the sun, which leaves the salt behind and returns the water as fresh rain.
questions.rationale: “Heated by the sun, seawater evaporates. The vapour rises up in the atmosphere, leaving behind the salt that the water had contained.”

questions.q: Many speak of God-realization (marifah) without attaining it. Why, according to the article?
options: It comes only in old age
Not quite. The article says: They wish for it but will not pay its price – giving themselves to it completely.
It requires great wealth
Not quite. The article says: They wish for it but will not pay its price – giving themselves to it completely.
They wish for it but will not pay its price – giving themselves to it completely
Yes. “Knowledge gives you a part of it only when you give yourself to it completely.”
It is granted only to scholars
Not quite. The article says: They wish for it but will not pay its price – giving themselves to it completely.
questions.rationale: “The reason is that they wish to attain the realization of God but they are not willing to pay the price… The price of God-realization is total surrender.”

questions.q: Can God-realization be handed down from father to son, in the article’s view?
options: No – it is personal and comes only through one’s own effort; otherwise it is merely traditional belief
Correct. A lifelong journey of discovery.
Yes, if the father is learned
Not quite. The article says: No – it is personal and comes only through one’s own effort; otherwise it is merely traditional belief.
Yes, in devout families
Not quite. The article says: No – it is personal and comes only through one’s own effort; otherwise it is merely traditional belief.
Only to the eldest child
Not quite. The article says: No – it is personal and comes only through one’s own effort; otherwise it is merely traditional belief.
questions.rationale: “Marifah… is not something to be inherited… Whatever one receives without personal struggle will be just a kind of traditional belief rather than a living marifah.”

questions.q: Science has found the universe to be well planned and well managed – even “intelligent.” What does the article say follows from this?
options: That it was shaped by human observers
Not quite. The article says: That it is the work of an intelligent Creator.
That it will run forever
Not quite. The article says: That it is the work of an intelligent Creator.
That it is the work of an intelligent Creator
Right. No other explanation fits.
That it needs no explanation
Not quite. The article says: That it is the work of an intelligent Creator.
questions.rationale: “Accepting the universe as an intelligent universe means also that this universe is the creation of an intelligent Creator.”

questions.q: Two people sit down to the same meal. What distinguishes the one the article calls “seeing” from the one it calls “blind”?
options: He knows the price of each item
Not quite. The article says: He recognises the food as God’s gift, the product of the whole universe, and feels wonder and gratitude.
He recognises the food as God’s gift, the product of the whole universe, and feels wonder and gratitude
Well reasoned. The other sees only shop-bought goods.
He has cooked the food himself
Not quite. The article says: He recognises the food as God’s gift, the product of the whole universe, and feels wonder and gratitude.
He eats more slowly
Not quite. The article says: He recognises the food as God’s gift, the product of the whole universe, and feels wonder and gratitude.
questions.rationale: “When he drinks milk, or puts a piece of fruit into his mouth, he feels that it is a unique blessing from God.”

questions.q: What does “faith in the unseen” mean, as the article explains it?
options: Ignoring the visible world
Not quite. The article says: Realising that what seems to come from human hands comes in truth from God.
Expecting miracles daily
Not quite. The article says: Realising that what seems to come from human hands comes in truth from God.
Realising that what seems to come from human hands comes in truth from God
Yes. Looking through appearance to reality.
Believing whatever one is told
Not quite. The article says: Realising that what seems to come from human hands comes in truth from God.
questions.rationale: “Faith in the unseen means the realization that the things which we seem to receive from the hands of men, come in actuality, from the hands of God.”

questions.q: We see or hear of a death almost daily. Why, says the article, do we fail to take in what it means?
options: Because it happens far away
Not quite. The article says: We are absorbed in worldly concerns and think of people only in worldly terms, not in relation to the eternal world.
Because the young are not told of it
Not quite. The article says: We are absorbed in worldly concerns and think of people only in worldly terms, not in relation to the eternal world.
Because death is rare
Not quite. The article says: We are absorbed in worldly concerns and think of people only in worldly terms, not in relation to the eternal world.
We are absorbed in worldly concerns and think of people only in worldly terms, not in relation to the eternal world
Exactly. No living picture of the Hereafter is before us.
questions.rationale: “We see man in relation to this ephemeral world, but fail to see him in relation to the next eternal world.”

questions.q: The commentary speaks of two ways of denying the Hereafter. What are they?
options: Denying it in words, and denying it in practice by living for this world alone
Well read. In effect the two are the same.
Denying it in private and in public
Not quite. The article says: Denying it in words, and denying it in practice by living for this world alone.
Denying it in youth and in old age
Not quite. The article says: Denying it in words, and denying it in practice by living for this world alone.
Denying it in prose and in verse
Not quite. The article says: Denying it in words, and denying it in practice by living for this world alone.
questions.rationale: “One group rejecting it by word of mouth and the other doing so in practice.”
